newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU floats ideas to curb massive olive oil fraud.
newsitem.headline: EU floats ideas to curb massive olive oil fraud.

text.p: Steps must be taken to reduce massive fraud over European Union olive oil subsidies and bring them into line with world free trade rules, EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said on Wednesday.
Olive oil fraud in southern EU producer countries is proportionately 10 times greater than for cereals and other crops, according to the EU's anti-fraud unit.
"Surely the European taxpayer is entitled to an effort on our part," Fischler told a news conference called to present a report on proposals to reform the system.
The reform is the latest in a series involving subsidies to farm produce begun in 1992 with cereals.
The controversial report was blocked for many months by southern countries who feared that planned changes would reduce farmers' revenues and lead to a decline in quality.
The EU spent 1.8 billion Ecus ($2.1 billion) last year in subsidising the EU's two million olive oil farmers in Italy, Greece, Spain, Portugal and France.
EU officials were unable to give a figure for how much of this involved fraud.
The 31-year-old olive oil market regime is one of the EU's oldest but it is also complex and over the years has shown itself to be open to abuse and almost impossible to control.

Pressure for reform has grown as the EU, the world's biggest olive oil producer with 80 percent of the market, faces a growing surplus which will have to be exported with the help of subsidies as new Spanish plantations become productive.
EU subsidised exports of 120,000 tonnes a year are already running over the level allowed under the world farm trade pact.
"If we fail to take action we will have structural surpluses that will increase annually," Fischler warned.
Fischler presented two options for reform.
The Commission's preferred move would be to link aid to the number of olive trees and historical regional yields.

"It would be easier to control, independent of production and more compatible with GATT rules," Fischler said, adding that member states would be allowed to attach environmental and other conditions. The olives would have to be marketed.

Fischler said that a census of EU olive trees -- estimated at around 460 million or considerably more than the number of EU citizens -- must be carried out before the new regime could take effect by the marketing year starting in November 1998.

The second option, favoured by most producers, would retain the current regime, based on production and consumption aids, but it would be simplifified by having a single system for small and large producers.

This would add a heavy burden of controlling small producers, accounting for two-thirds of the total, Fischler noted. Previously they were subsidised on the basis of the number and production potential of their olive trees.
National output limits would be imposed and subsidies progressively reduced for production overruns.
The Commission will draft a proposal for approval by EU farm ministers after it has received reactions to the report from the olive oil trade and industry and the European Parliament.
